title: Review queue replay with rework escalation
scenario: Replay an out-of-order event log through a claim/submit/approve/reject state machine with rework escalation at 3 rejections, then report per-person tables and queue-health numbers.

verified.why_correct: `rework >= MAX_REWORK` looks like it should be `>`, but the spec escalates when the rework count *reaches* 3, i.e. on the third rejection. T04 is rejected exactly three times and must end escalated.
It tries exactly the three formats the README lists, with month/day order for the slash format, and raises on anything else.

bugs.title: History list shared by every task
bugs.old:
closed_at = None

    def __init__(self, task_id, queue, created_at):
        self.task_id = task_id
        self.queue = queue
        self.created_at = created_at
        self.history = []
bugs.new:
closed_at = None
    history = []

    def __init__(self, task_id, queue, created_at):
        self.task_id = task_id
        self.queue = queue
        self.created_at = created_at
bugs.symptom: Test 1 test_transition_counts: every task reports 34 transitions (the total number of applied events) instead of 3, 6, 3, 9, ... Nothing else changes.
bugs.why: `history = []` at class level is a single list object shared by every TaskRecord. `task.history.append(...)` mutates that one list, so every task sees every applied event. The scalar class defaults (state, rework) are safe only because they are reassigned, never mutated.
hints: Every task reports the same number of transitions. What would make that happen?
Look at where TaskRecord's history list is created.
`history = []` is a class attribute; create it in __init__ as `self.history = []`.
probes: Why are `state = State.QUEUED` and `rework = 0` safe as class attributes when `history = []` is not?
What does `task.rework += 1` do to the class attribute, and why?

bugs.title: Same-time events ordered by id string
bugs.symptom: Test 1: T05 ends 'claimed' instead of 'submitted' with 1 transition, and E12 heads the invalid list. Test 2: ann-02 has 3 submissions instead of 4. Test 3: state_counts shows claimed 2 / submitted 1.
bugs.why: Event ids are strings, and `"E12" < "E8"` lexicographically. E8 (claim) and E12 (submit) on T05 share a timestamp, so the submit is replayed first against a queued task and rejected.
bugs.unblocks: T05 in test_1_lifecycle, and the invalid list.
hints: T05 ends up claimed and E12 is listed as invalid. Look at E8 and E12 in events.csv.
How are events with the same timestamp ordered?
Sort by `(ev.at, ev.seq)`; seq is the integer event number.
probes: Why did other same-timestamp pairs (E33/E36, E34/E40) not change anything?
Would zero-padding the ids in the data have hidden this? Why is that not a real fix?

bugs.title: Review state compared to a string
bugs.symptom: Every approve and reject is invalid. Test 1: all reviewed tasks stay 'submitted', T04 never escalates, the invalid list has 21 ids. Test 2: reviewer and annotator approval counts are all 0. Test 3: first_pass_rate and avg_cycle_hours are None, submitted = 8.
bugs.why: `State` is a plain Enum, so `State.SUBMITTED != "submitted"` is always True. Every approve and reject is treated as invalid and no task ever leaves `submitted`.
bugs.unblocks: Most of test_1 and test_2, and exposes B5 and B6 in test_3.
hints: No task is ever approved or rejected. Which check do both actions share?
Look at how `_reviewable` compares the task's state.
Compare against the enum: `task.state is not State.SUBMITTED`.
probes: Would this comparison have worked if State subclassed `str`?
Why did avg_cycle_hours come out as None rather than a wrong number?

bugs.title: Any role can review
bugs.symptom: Test 1: E13 is invalid instead of E11 (ann-01's approval of T03 is accepted). Test 2: annotators ann-01..ann-05 appear in the reviewers table and rev-02 has 1 approval instead of 2. Test 3: avg_cycle_hours 24.2 instead of 24.5.
bugs.why: `a == b or "lead"` parses as `(a == b) or "lead"`, which is the truthy string "lead" for every non-reviewer. Annotators pass the review check, so ann-01's approval of T03 (E11) is applied.
hints: Annotators appear in the reviewers table. Who decides who can review?
probes: What value does the buggy expression return for an annotator?
Why did E13 become invalid once E11 was accepted?

bugs.title: Cycle time ignores whole days
bugs.symptom: Only visible once B3 is fixed. Test 3 test_avg_cycle_hours: 5.3 instead of 24.5.
bugs.why: `timedelta.seconds` is only the seconds part after whole days are removed. T02 (50 h) counts as 2 h and T08 (54 h) as 6 h.
hints: Which approved tasks took more than a day? Do their cycle times look right?
Look at how cycle_hours turns a timedelta into hours.
probes: Why was this invisible while approvals were failing?

bugs.title: First-pass count taken over all tasks
bugs.old: first_pass = [t for t in approved if t.rework == 0]
bugs.new: first_pass = [t for t in tasks.values() if t.rework == 0]
bugs.symptom: Only visible once B3 is fixed, and only in Test 3: first_pass_rate is 2.0 instead of 0.8.
bugs.why: The numerator counts every task with no rework, including queued and claimed ones, while the denominator is approved tasks only, so the rate goes above 1.

context_qa.q: What does build_report() do, step by step?
context_qa.a: It loads members.json, tasks.csv and events.csv through loader.py, calls `engine.replay` to apply the events to the TaskRecords in place, then builds the task table, the invalid list, `metrics.reviewer_table`, `metrics.annotator_table` and `reports.summarize`.

context_qa.q: How does replay decide an event is invalid?
context_qa.a: It looks up the task, the actor and the handler for the action. If any is missing, or the actor is inactive, the event id goes to `invalid`. Otherwise it calls the handler from `transitions.HANDLERS`; a False return also marks it invalid. Applied events are appended to `task.history` and to the `applied` list.

context_qa.q: What is Event.seq and where is it set?
context_qa.a: An integer parsed from the event id with the leading `E` stripped (`E12` becomes 12). It is set in `loader.load_events`, which also sorts the events before returning them.

context_qa.q: Which attributes does TaskRecord set in __init__ and which come from the class?
context_qa.a: Look at `models.TaskRecord`: the class body declares defaults for state, rework, assignee, submitter and closed_at (and any other class-level names), and `__init__` assigns task_id, queue, created_at plus whatever else it sets on `self`.
It is a property that returns the result of an expression over `self.role`. `transitions._reviewable` wraps it in `bool()` and `metrics.reviewer_table` uses it to choose which members get a row.

context_qa.q: How is the annotator `approved` count computed?
context_qa.a: `annotator_table` walks the tasks and, for each task in the APPROVED state, adds one to the row of `task.submitter`, which `transitions.submit` sets to the actor of the last applied submit.

context_qa.q: What are the units of cycle_hours?
context_qa.a: It subtracts `created_at` from `closed_at` (both datetimes from parse_when) and divides a seconds value by 3600. `summarize` averages it over approved tasks and rounds to 2 decimals.
